problems.stem: How is the AI 'responsibility gap' (Matthias 2004) most defensibly closed?
options: By attributing moral responsibility to the AI system itself.

By distributing responsibility across the human chain (developer, deployer, operator, user) so no link can hide behind another link's opacity, with role-specific failure ownership documented in advance.
By assigning all responsibility to the user.
problems.explanation: Machines are not moral agents under any major framework. The gap is closed by structured human accountability, not by anthropomorphizing the system.

problems.stem: Under the capacity-time-authority-information test, when is human-in-the-loop oversight meaningful?
options: Whenever a human is formally part of the workflow.
When the human reviewer has capacity to understand, time sufficient for the stakes, authority to override without penalty, and information beyond the bare recommendation.
When the override rate is exactly 5%.
Only when the model is interpretable.
problems.explanation: EU AI Act Art. 14 and the oversight literature agree on these four conditions. Without them, the human-in-the-loop is structural fig leaf.

problems.stem: Which engineering practice is most directly tied to making accountability survive turnover and lawsuits?
options: Audit trails that log every consequential decision with model version, input, score, threshold, and human override, retained long enough to be reviewable a year later.
problems.explanation: Audit trails are the artifact accountability lives in. Without them, post-hoc accountability claims are unverifiable.

problems.stem: What is the purpose of model cards (Mitchell et al. 2019) and datasheets for datasets (Gebru et al. 2018) in an accountability framework?
options: Documented disclosure of intended use, known limitations, training-data summaries, and performance disaggregated by subgroup — discharging the failure-to-warn duty and supporting downstream deployer review.
problems.explanation: Model cards and datasheets operationalize the failure-to-warn doctrine and let deployers make informed decisions about fit-for-purpose.
